Definition
Without input or output devices, a microprocessor system has no way of communicating with the outside world.
INTRODUCTIONM
There are numerous input and output devices available today to solve this problem.
In this lesson, we are going to look at how IO (input/output) devices are connected to the 8086, the different types of devices, and examples of their implementation.
Let's begin the lesson on INTERFACING WITH THE 8086 MICROPROCESSOR..........
LESSON MENU
INTERFACING WITH 8086
MICROPROCESSOR
In the previous lesson we looked at the connection of memory to the 8086 microprocessor. The connection of IO devices is very similar to the connection of memory.
DISCUSSION
Let's look at the signals necessary for the connection of the IO to the 8086. The graphic below shows only the signals used to connect the 8086 microprocessor to the IO.
Many of these signals are used for memory circuit connections. As far as connecting to the 8086, the connections are very similar. The main difference is how they are accessed through assembly code.

Notice there are only 16 address lines used. The 8086 was designed to only allow the use of 65536 IO devices. Since most computers do not use more than 100 devices, it is rare that an IO address requires a segment.
Also provided to IO devices are 16 data lines used to transfer information. The direction of data transfer from IO to the microprocessor is controlled by the WR and RD pins just as memory is.

The ASTB pin is used for the address latches and the BUFEN and BUF/R/W for the address buffers. The IO/M pin is what selects between IO and memory. When this pin is low, it indicates that IO is being accessed.
IO is arranged in the same way as memory chips. Each address combination of the 8086 address lines can be used by a different device. Most devices will take a range of addresses, not just one.

These different addresses use different functions of the device. When we look at the operation of the parallel port IO device we will see this type of setup. The graphic below shows the connection of a few IO devices to an 8086 microprocessor.
Now that you understand the basic memory connection of IO circuits, which is very similar to the way memory is connected, let's look at different devices connected to the 8086.
IO devices fall into one of three categories: input, output, or input/output devices. They are further categorized as being either fixed or removable devices.

Fixed IO devices are permanently connected to the system. Removable IO devices are connected to a microprocessor through a special universal connection port. These ports are designed for many different types of IO.
Examples of fixed IO devices are the keyboard and display of the Nida 8086 trainer. Removable IO devices would be connected to either the serial or parallel or ports.
Let's look at an example of each type of device to understand their communication with the microprocessor.

Input devices allow information to be sent to the microprocessor or to control it in some fashion. A keyboard, for example, can be used to select options, program new instructions, or make modifications to old programs.
MICROPROCESSOR
Input devices include: a mouse, lightpen, trackball, scanner, or keyboard, to name a few. The only "Input Only" device on the 8086 microprocessor trainer is the keyboard.

Input means that the device does not provide any outputs to the user. To better understand the operation of an input device, let's look at the actual circuitry used to control the keyboard in the 8086 microprocessor trainer.

The keyboard has been broken down into five main sections: the keyboard matrix, the keyboard latch, the keyboard buffer, the key decoding circuit, and the control circuit. Below is the block diagram of the keyboard and its associated circuitry.
KEYBOARD
KEYBOARD BUFFER
ADDRESS BUSS
Let's start by looking at the keyboard key matrix. oard matrix, buffer and the key decoding circuit. Let's start by looking at the keyboard key matrix.
KEYBOARD MATRIX
The keyboard matrix is an arrangement of horizontal and vertical wires with switches connected across them.
Pressing any one key connects two wires, one horizontal and one vertical. Each key has its own connection making them unique to one another.
By sending a signal through a horizontal wire, the vertical wires can be looked at to see which key in that row was pressed, if any. This brings us to the next circuit, the keyboard latch.
KEYBOARD LATCH
The keyboard latch is an 8-bit latch connected to the 8 horizontal connections of the keyboard key matrix.
The output of a latch is the last input present when the clock pulse came through. The data bus of the 8086 is used to send and receive signals from the keyboard circuitry.
Since we cannot send and receive at the same time, a latch provides a way of holding a previous set of signals from the data bus to allow the results of these applied signals to be read.

When a key is pressed, a program in the microprocessor sets the latch to output all highs to all horizontal lines, except for one, which it sets to low. The program then checks to see if that low is present on any of the vertical lines.
If none are found, the horizontal line is set to high and the next one is set to low. The process or loop in which each line is repeatedly set and tested is known as polling........................

It is important to note that a program in the microprocessor performs many steps in controlling the keyboard, not just the associated circuitry. This program is contained within the monitor program used by the 8086 microprocessor.
KEYBOARD BUFFER
The five vertical lines of the keyboard matrix are connected to the first five inputs of the keyboard buffer. Notice also that each of the five lines are connected to Vcc through a resistor.
When none of the keys are being pressed on the keyboard, there is a HIGH signal on each of the vertical lines. This is because +5V is connected to each line through a resistor.

If a key is pressed on a row where the horizontal line is HIGH, then a HIGH will be connected to the associated vertical line and to the buffer. This condition would cause the microprocessor not to be able to recognize the keystroke.

If a key is pressed on a row where the horizontal line is LOW, then a LOW will be connected to the bottom of the resistor and to the buffer. The resistor has to be large enough to allow all of +5V to be dropped across it without damage............
Without the resistor, +5V would be connected to ground, damaging the power source.
KEY DECODING CIRCUIT

The key decoding circuit, as shown below, only allows the microprocessor to register the pressed key once before generating the needed interrupt signal. While the key is being held down it doesn't allow its circuits to reset.

This low condition indicates a pressed key to the microprocessor. At this point you are probably wondering if, when a key is pressed, is there a possibility that the horizontal line may not go low during that time?
No need to worry. The process of making each line low, one at a time, happens approximately 40 times a second. When you press a key the microprocessor will be able to be notified many times.
This brings up another important point: will not the microprocessor think that the key was pressed many times? hen you press a key, the microprocessor will be notified many times.
The key decoding circuit only allows the microprocessor to register the key you've pressed once. While the key is being held down it doesn't allow its circuits to reset.

All of the components of the key decoding circuit are contained within an IC known as a GAL (Generic Array Logic). This IC can be programmed to represent many different logic circuits connected in a multitude of ways.
The purpose for using this IC is to save room on the circuit cards. If individual IC's were used for all the logic components of the GAL, it would take up much more room.

The D type flip-flop in the GAL representation schematic sets and notifies the microprocessor when a key is depressed. The flip-flop resets when the key is released. The combination logic used in determining whether a key has been pressed or released is also contained within the GAL.fffffffffff
CONTROL CIRCUIT

This is the last section of the keyboard circuits. This circuit is controlled by the microprocessor which in turn controls all functions of the keyboard circuitry. The three main control signals applied by the microprocessor are: IOCS1, A2, and WR. RD, the other control signal required for reading the keyboard, is applied directly to pin 19 of the keyboard buffer.

RD, the other control signal required for reading the keyboard, is applied directly to pin 19 of the keyboard buffer.

These four lines tell the circuit to be active, inactive, reading or writing, just to name a few. The output of the IO chip select circuitry is connected to the keyboard control circuit. This way, only the keyboard will be active when the microprocessor is reading or writing data to this device.
The IO chip select is actually combined with the memory chip select in the 8086 circuitry. The IO/M signal is the important signal which distinguishes between memory and IO.
As you can see, there are many different sections to even a simple input device. The actual complexity of an input device will depend on its purpose.
If the keyboard had consisted of only one key it would have probably been connected directly to the microprocessor and that would have been the entire circuit.
Now that we have looked at an input device, let's look at an output device.
MICROPROCESSOR

While input devices allow you to input information into a microprocessor system, output devices allow you to see or receive feedback from the microprocessor about operations, data, or performance.................
An output device could be a printer, phone line, or display of some sort. Many microprocessor systems have outputs to monitors, or LCD displays.
To get a better understanding of output devices, let's look at the operation of the LCD display of the 8086 microprocessor trainer.
DATA SIGNALS
INTENSITY

LCD is an acronym which stands for Liquid Crystal Display, which also describes the technique of how the display works. A liquid crystal display has an actual liquid crystal in between two pieces of glass.
Transparent, conductive materials are used to apply voltage to the liquid crystal. When voltage is applied, the crystals in the liquid scatter and do not allow light to pass through the glass.
In the rear portion of the glass, holding the liquid crystal, a reflective surface shines light backwards through the glass illuminating the characters.

The LCD unit, like the one on the PC130-404 card, has fourteen pins and its own processor for interfacing with the 8086 microprocessor. The self contained processor, under the control of the 8086 microprocesor, drives the LCD and provides all functions necessary for proper display.
Vss and Vdd are used to power the LCD module. The capacitor between them is used to protect the circuit from voltages spikes. Vcc is used to set the intensity of the display.
You can see that this pin is connected to a potentiometer with one side connected to 5 volts and the other to ground. Adjusting the potentiometer will adjust the display intensity.

The next three connections of the LCD module are control lines. The control lines are the RS (register Select), R/W (Read/Not Write) and the E (Enable) pins. There are two types of memory within the display unit; character memory and display memory.
Character memory holds all the information about the displayable characters and the user definable characters. User definable characters means that you can assign them to whatever function you want.

Character memory is split into two sections; RAM and ROM. The character RAM, also known as the CG RAM, holds all of the user defined character codes. If you create your own characters you must reload them into the display every time you turn the display module on...............

This is because, the CG memory space is RAM which is erased every time power is removed from the system. The character ROM, known as the CG ROM, holds all the permanent information about the predefined unchangeable characters of the display module.
Data books written about the displays will illustrate the predefined characters, how they are organized, and also indicate which characters can be changed.
The display RAM, known as the DD RAM, is used to hold the current information that is being displayed on the LCD screen. There isn't any DD ROM because it isn't necessary.
All areas of the screen are fully programmable. The last eight lines of the display module connections are data lines. These lines are used to input information to the display module.
Now that we have looked at the input and output devices, let's look at some common circuits which employ both methods of communication, input and output.
INPUT/OUTPUT (I/O))
MICROPROCESSOR

The two most common forms of input/output are the serial and parallel ports. Ports are connectors in a system used to interface external devices. External devices could be modems, printers, scanners, ect.
An I/O port allows you to hook up any these using a standardized protocol, either serial or parallel. There are other types of standard connections, however, they are not a part of this 8086 system.
Only the most common types of ports have been integrated into the system.
The names serial and parallel describe the type of communication that occurs. Serial connections require, at a minimum, three connections for two-way communication: send, receive, and ground. nd.
SERIAL PORT

In some systems more connections are provided for certain types of control and protection. However, in most cases these types of signals aren't needed. Serial indicates that, at any given time, only one data bit can be sent.

If you were sending 8-bits of data, it would take 8 sends to completely transmit the bits. The advantage of serial communications is that it only requires a few wires, so it's well adapted for telephone transmission.

Parallel communication, used mostly with printers, is the sending of many bits at once. Normally, 8-bits are sent, each on their own line. Additional lines are also provided for control and protection.
PARALLEL PORT
PARALLEL PORT CONNECTIONS

The parallel port is faster than the serial port because of this simultaneous transfer of data. This increased speed however, comes at a cost. Increased cost for multiple conductor cable, more complex circuitry, and signal degradation as cable lengths increase, all combine to limit the length of parallel data cables to lengths shorter than serial data cables.

Frequently, printers are located close to the computer making the use of the parallel port for interconnection ideal. On some systems the parallel port is called the printer port, on others it is called LPT. to allow it to travel longer distances.

In some situations, certain devices need the speed of the parallel port and the distance of the serial port. Special devices exist that can amplify the signals of the parallel port allowing them to travel greater distances.

Another type of I/O device, which hasn't been implemented into the 8086 system you are using, is networking. It hasn't been implemented because this trainer does not need to be networked, however, the principle is important.

Networking is the connection of many computers together to provide interaction with resources and users. There are many different types of protocols and configurations, however, their main purpose is the same.
Computers connected to the Internet are connected through some sort of networking device. Computer programs are designed to allow many different computers to have their I/O ports connected together.
If one computer sends information, each of the other computers on a network can look to see if they are supposed to read that data.
As the Internet grows larger and larger, communication ports may change to accommodate the different needs associated with this type of communication.
However, the principles of their operation will closely relate to the most common interface ports, serial and parallel.
